_meta.purpose: The ergonomic layer — the body, before any room exists. This is the level Neufert works at: percentile body dimensions, reach envelopes, the space an activity occupies. Everything above it (space types, clearances, validation rules) is derived from these numbers rather than asserted independently, so changing a user group's reach propagates through every rule that depends on it.
_meta.provenance_policy: Seeded from freely citable sources. `neufert_ref` is an empty slot on every record for you to fill from your own copy of Architects' Data for internal verification. Do NOT paste Neufert tables here — this repository is meant to be shareable and the work is copyrighted. Cite the regulation or standard as the published source; use Neufert to catch what you forgot to model.
_meta.percentile_note: P5 is used for REACH (design for the shortest reach so everyone can reach) and P95 for CLEARANCE (design for the largest body so everyone fits). Using P50 for both is the classic ergonomic error: it designs for a person who does not exist and excludes half the population at each end.

envelopes.label: Older adult, ambulant
envelopes.gait_note: Reduced reach range in BOTH directions. The comfortable band narrows from roughly 400-1700 mm to 500-1500 mm, which is why storage designed for a younger body becomes unusable rather than merely inconvenient.

envelopes.label: Older adult with rollator
envelopes.note: Occupied depth includes the device in front of the body. This is why a rollator user needs more than a wheelchair user at a counter, not less.

envelopes.label: Manual wheelchair user
envelopes.note: The reach band 400-1200 mm is the single most useful number in accessible design. Anything a person must operate - switch, handle, socket, shelf, hob control - belongs inside it. Most standard kitchens put half their storage outside it.

envelopes.label: Care resident requiring assistance
envelopes.note: Reach is barely relevant: most tasks are performed BY someone else. The binding dimensions belong to the assisting staff, which is why staff_care must be modelled as a user group in its own right rather than folded in.

envelopes.label: Care staff at work
envelopes.note: A legally recognised user group in Sweden. Working space around a bed is an occupational-health requirement, not a comfort preference, and cannot be value-engineered away.

envelopes.label: Child, 3-5 years
envelopes.note: Eye height 970 mm sets vision panels and sill heights. The floor is a working surface at this age, which changes what a finish has to do.

activity_zones._note: The space an ACTIVITY occupies, not the object. This is the layer that turns furniture into a plan: a bed is 900x2000, but sleeping-and-getting-out-of-bed is considerably more, and only the second number tells you whether a room works.

zones.label: Stand and turn on the spot
Stand at an open wardrobe door
Seated at a table, chair pushed back to stand
Bending to a low oven or appliance
Making a bed from one side
Two staff assisting at a bed
Seated at a table, side position
zones.note: Per seat along a table edge. Below 700 mm of width per person, elbows collide.

zones.label: Passing behind a seated person
zones.note: Measured from the table edge: 800 mm for the chair pushed back, plus 300 mm to squeeze past. Make it 1200 mm where people pass often, and 1500 mm where a wheelchair passes. This is the dimension that decides whether a dining area works, and it is almost never drawn.

zones.label: Legroom in front of a sofa
zones.note: Sofa face to coffee table. Below 400 mm you cannot get in; above 600 mm you cannot reach the table.

zones.label: Passing in front of seated people
Rising from a low seat
zones.note: Older adults and anyone with reduced strength push forward and down on the armrests. The zone in front must be clear, not occupied by a coffee table.

zones.label: Working at a hob
zones.note: Needs a heat-safe landing surface each side; the depth is for turning with a hot pan.

zones.label: Between two facing kitchen runs
zones.note: 1200 mm for one cook with drawers open. 1500 mm where two people work, and 1500 mm for a wheelchair to turn between runs. Under 1000 mm opposing drawers collide.

zones.label: Beside a WC, transfer side
zones.note: One side for independent wheelchair use, both sides for assisted care. The most commonly omitted requirement in small-apartment plans, and it cannot be retrofitted without moving drainage.

zones.label: Drying and dressing after washing
zones.note: Routinely forgotten. A wet room that meets every fixture clearance and has nowhere to stand and dry is a wet room people dress in the hall.

zones.label: Beside a door, pull side
zones.note: Space to stand beside the handle while the door opens towards you. Without it a wheelchair user cannot open the door at all.

heights._note: Working and operating heights. These are derived from the body rather than listed per room: a counter height IS the user's standing work surface, a light switch IS somewhere inside their reach band. Deriving them means a change of user group moves every height in the building at once, which is what you want and what a lookup table cannot do.

rules.label: Kitchen worktop
rules.note: For a seated user this must be a knee-clearance counter, not just a lower one: the height means nothing without 700 mm of clear space beneath it to get your knees under.

rules.label: WC seat
rules.note: Raised to 480 mm for transfer and for anyone who struggles to rise. Standard domestic pans sit at 400-420 mm.

rules.label: Socket outlet
rules.note: Skirting-level sockets are outside the reach band of every seated user. Lifting them to 400 mm costs nothing at first fit and is impossible to change later without chasing walls.

rules.label: Highest shelf worth using
rules.note: Everything above this line is storage you own and cannot use. In a standard kitchen that is usually the top two shelves of every wall cabinet.

rules.label: Window sill, for a seated view
rules.note: A maximum, not a target. Eye above sill is not a view — the sightline has to reach the ground nearby rather than the sky.

layout_standards._note: Area and spacing rules that apply to a whole arrangement rather than a single object. These are the numbers you would otherwise estimate.

dining.note: Area per seat covers the table share plus the chair plus getting out of it. 1.6 m² is a banquet figure; tight domestic dining runs at 1.2 and feels it.

living.note: Conversation fails beyond about 2.7 m between seats — people raise their voices and stop talking. It is the most reliable predictor of whether a living room gets used, and it is a spacing rule, not an area rule.

kitchen.note: The work triangle is sink-hob-fridge. Under 3.6 m total you are cramped, over 6.6 m you are walking. Landing surfaces beside hob and sink are where hot pans and wet dishes go, and omitting them is why some kitchens feel unusable despite plenty of counter.

bathroom.note: Fixture centreline spacing, not edge clearance. 400 mm from WC centreline to a side wall is the absolute minimum for sitting; 450 is comfortable.

turning._note: Manoeuvring space by device and level. Swedish practice distinguishes normalniva (dwellings) from hojd niva (raised level, public and care settings), which is why one number will not do.
